Question: The students in Mr. Neatkin’s class took a penmanship test. Two-thirds of the boys and \(\frac{3}{4}\) of the girls passed the test, and an equal number of boys and girls passed the test. What is the minimum possible number of students in the class?
Solution:
Let \(p\) be the number of boys who passed, which is also the number of girls who passed. Since the class is nonempty and both passing fractions are positive, \(p>0\).

For two-thirds of the boys to be a whole number, the number of boys must be a multiple of \(3\). Each group of \(3\) boys contributes \(2\) passing boys, so \(p\) must be a multiple of \(2\). Similarly, the girls come in groups of \(4\), each contributing \(3\) passing girls, so \(p\) must also be a multiple of \(3\).

The smallest positive common multiple of \(2\) and \(3\) is \(6\). With \(6\) passing students from each group, the required group sizes are
\[
6\div\frac23=9\text{ boys},
\]
\[
6\div\frac34=8\text{ girls}.
\]
These counts work because two-thirds of \(9\) and three-fourths of \(8\) both equal \(6\). Any larger common passing count requires more students in both groups. Therefore the minimum class size is \(9+8=17\), choice \(\mathrm{B}\).
